subject: Physics
title: Magnetism and Matter
summary: The bar magnet as a magnetic dipole, its equivalence to a current-carrying solenoid, torque and energy of a dipole in a uniform field, Gauss's law for magnetism, and how matter responds to a magnetic field (magnetisation, susceptibility, permeability; dia-, para- and ferromagnetism). It is a short chapter that reliably gives one or two 1-mark questions and a 2- or 3-mark question on magnetic materials, and it pairs with Chapter 4 for the 5-mark and case-based questions.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit III (Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism: Chapters 4 and 5) carries 17 marks together with Unit IV (Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents). Chapter 5 alone typically contributes 3 to 5 marks: one or two 1-mark questions (MCQ or Assertion-Reason on magnetic materials or field lines), and one 2- or 3-mark question on classifying materials, torque on a dipole, or a solenoid-as-magnet numerical. Long derivations from this chapter are less common than from Chapter 4, but the compass-needle SHM and the equivalent-solenoid derivation have been asked.

question_types.note: Identify a material from its susceptibility or relative permeability; the ratio of axial to equatorial field; what happens to magnetic moment when a magnet is cut or bent; the orientation of stable and unstable equilibrium; the susceptibility of a superconductor; net magnetic flux through a closed surface.

Field lines form closed loops because monopoles do not exist; diamagnetism is temperature independent; paramagnetic susceptibility falls with temperature; a superconductor is a perfect diamagnet; a magnet cut along its length has half the moment.

Define susceptibility, permeability, magnetisation or magnetic intensity with SI units; state two properties of field lines; how a dia- and a paramagnetic sample behave in a non-uniform field; ratio of moments when a coil is rewound; why a solenoid behaves like a bar magnet.

Derive the torque on a dipole and the potential energy; compute H, M and B in a solenoid with a core; distinguish dia-, para- and ferromagnetic materials on three points with field-line sketches; state and explain Gauss's law for magnetism; compute the axial and equatorial fields of a short magnet.

A passage on magnetic materials (susceptibility table, superconductors, Curie temperature) or on a solenoid acting as a magnet, with four 1-mark sub-parts that are usually MCQs or one-line answers.

sections.heading: 5.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Magnetism was known long before electricity. The word comes from Magnesia, a district in Greece where the mineral magnetite (lodestone, Fe3O4) was found; the Chinese used lodestone compasses for navigation more than two thousand years ago. NCERT opens the chapter with a handful of facts that every later section builds on, and the examiner assumes you know them.

First, the earth behaves as a magnet. Its field lines point, roughly, from the geographic south to the geographic north, so the end of a freely suspended magnet that points towards geographic north is called the north pole of the magnet. Second, a bar magnet has two poles, north and south; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Third, and this is the fact behind Gauss's law for magnetism, magnetic poles never occur singly. If you cut a magnet into two you do not get an isolated north and an isolated south; you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles. Isolated magnetic charges (monopoles) have never been observed. Fourth, you can make a magnet from an iron bar by keeping it in a magnetic field or by stroking it with a magnet, and some materials keep the magnetism once the field is removed.

The chapter then does three things. It treats the bar magnet as a magnetic dipole, exactly parallel to the electric dipole of Chapter 1, and shows that a current-carrying solenoid is the same kind of object. It states Gauss's law for magnetism. And it asks how a piece of matter responds when placed in a magnetic field, which leads to magnetisation, susceptibility, permeability and the three classes of magnetic materials. Note that in the rationalised NCERT text the sections on the earth's magnetism (declination, dip), hysteresis, and permanent magnets and electromagnets have been dropped, so the board paper does not ask them. Older question banks still contain them; do not waste revision time there.
sections.tip: If a 1-mark question asks why a freely suspended magnet settles along north-south, answer that the earth's magnetic field exerts a torque on the magnet until its moment is along the field; do not say the earth pulls the north pole.

sections.heading: 5.2 The Bar Magnet
sections.body:
Sprinkle iron filings on a sheet placed over a bar magnet and they arrange themselves in curved lines that bunch near the two ends. Those ends are the poles. The same pattern is produced by a current-carrying solenoid, which is the first hint that a bar magnet and a solenoid are the same physical object seen from outside.

NCERT describes a bar magnet by a magnetic moment m, a vector directed from the south pole to the north pole inside the magnet. If the pole strength is qm and the magnetic length is 2l (the distance between the poles, a little less than the geometric length), then m = qm × 2l. The SI unit of m is A m2, which is the same as J T−1. Pole strength has the unit A m. You do not need to derive anything with qm; it matters only for the cut-the-magnet questions.

Two facts about cutting and bending a magnet are asked again and again. Cut a magnet transverse to its length into two equal halves: each piece keeps the same pole strength qm, its length becomes l, so its moment becomes m/2. Cut it along its length: each half has half the cross-section, so its pole strength becomes qm/2, its length stays 2l, and its moment is again m/2. Bend a magnet of length L and moment m into a semicircle: the pole strength is unchanged, but the poles are now a chord 2R = 2L/π apart, so the new moment is 2m/π. A magnetic needle placed near a magnet aligns along the field of the magnet; this is how the field pattern is mapped point by point.

where: magnetic moment, directed S to N inside the magnet (A m<sup>2</sup> or J T<sup>−1</sup>)
magnetic length, the separation of the poles

formulas.expr: Magnet bent into a semicircle: m' = 2m/π
where: moment of the straight magnet of length L

sections.tip: Whatever way you cut a magnet, each piece has a moment less than the original; the piece never ends up with a single pole. Write which quantity (pole strength or length) halves; the examiner looks for that reasoning, not just the answer m/2.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 The magnetic field lines
sections.body:
Magnetic field lines are the pictorial way of showing the field B, and NCERT lists their properties in four points that you should be able to write from memory.

  1. The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous closed loops. Outside the magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole; inside the magnet they continue from the south pole back to the north pole. This is the key difference from electric field lines, which begin on positive charges and end on negative charges and are never closed loops.
  2. The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the net magnetic field B at that point.
  3. The larger the number of field lines crossing per unit area, the larger the magnitude of B. The lines are crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest.
  4. Field lines never intersect. If they did, the field would have two directions at the crossing point, which is impossible.

The field-line pictures for a bar magnet and for a finite solenoid look identical from outside, and the field of an electric dipole has the same shape outside the dipole. Only inside do they differ: inside the magnet the lines run S to N to close the loop, while between the charges of an electric dipole the field runs from positive to negative, opposite to the dipole moment direction. NCERT points out that field lines are not really lines of force; a compass needle placed on a line experiences a torque, not a force along the line.

When the exam asks you to draw the field lines of a bar magnet, draw the loops passing through the magnet, mark N and S, put arrows N to S outside and S to N inside, and make the lines closer together near the poles. A sketch without the inside lines loses a mark because it fails to show the closed-loop property.
sections.tip: The one-line answer for why magnetic field lines are closed: magnetic monopoles do not exist, so lines have nowhere to start or end. Pair this with Gauss's law when the question is for 2 marks.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
sections.body:
Ampere's hypothesis is that all magnetic phenomena come from circulating currents. The evidence in this chapter is that the field of a bar magnet, at points far away, has exactly the form of the field of a solenoid, and both are dipole fields. The rationalised syllabus asks only for a qualitative treatment, but the derivation is short and has been asked in the past, so learn the steps.

Take a solenoid of radius a, length 2l, n turns per unit length and current I, with its centre at the origin and its axis along x. Consider a thin slice of the solenoid of thickness dx at a distance x from the centre; it contains n dx turns and acts as a circular coil. From Chapter 4, the field of this slice at a point P on the axis at distance r from the centre is dB = μ0 (n dx) I a2 / 2[(r − x)2 + a2]3/2. For a point far from the solenoid, r ≫ a and r ≫ l, so the denominator becomes simply 2r3 and dB ≈ μ0 n I a2 dx / 2r3. Integrating x from −l to +l gives the total field on the axis:

B = μ0 n I a2 (2l) / 2r3 = (μ0/4π) · 2 [n (2l) I (πa2)] / r3 = (μ0/4π) · 2m/r3,

where m = n(2l) I (πa2) = N I A is the magnetic moment of the solenoid (N total turns, area A). This is exactly the axial field of a bar magnet of moment m. So a solenoid behaves like a bar magnet with moment NIA, directed along its axis in the sense given by the right-hand rule (curl the fingers along the current, the thumb points to the north face). NCERT confirms the equivalence experimentally: a suspended solenoid settles N-S like a magnet, and it attracts or repels another magnet just as a bar magnet does.

Two exam uses follow. A short-answer question gives N, I and A and asks for m and then the torque in a field. A conceptual question asks how a solenoid is like a bar magnet: same field pattern outside, both have a north and a south face, both experience the same torque in a field, and the solenoid's poles reverse when the current reverses.

formulas.expr: m = N I A (solenoid or coil)

where: distance of the point from the centre on the axis

sections.tip: In the derivation, state the two approximations r ≫ a and r ≫ l explicitly before you simplify the denominator. That is the step the marking scheme rewards.

sections.heading: 5.2.3 The dipole in a uniform magnetic field
sections.body:
Place a small compass needle of moment m and moment of inertia I in a uniform field B, with m making an angle θ with B. Think of the needle as two poles ±qm separated by 2l: the field pushes the north pole along B and the south pole opposite to B with equal forces qmB. The net force is zero, so the needle does not move as a whole, but the two forces form a couple of arm 2l sin θ. The torque is τ = qmB × 2l sin θ = mB sin θ, and as a vector τ = m × B. The torque tends to align m with B. It is zero at θ = 0 (stable equilibrium) and θ = 180° (unstable equilibrium), and maximum, τ = mB, at θ = 90°.

Oscillations. Displace the needle by a small angle θ and release it. The restoring torque gives I d2θ/dt2 = −mB sin θ. For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, so d2θ/dt2 = −(mB/I) θ. This is the SHM equation with ω2 = mB/I, so the time period is T = 2π√(I/mB). Rearranging, B = 4π2I/(mT2), which is how a vibration magnetometer measures a field. This full argument, from the couple to the period, is the standard 5-mark derivation from this chapter.

Potential energy. The work done by an external agent in turning the dipole from θ1 to θ2 is W = ∫ mB sin θ dθ = mB (cos θ1 − cos θ2). Taking the zero of energy at θ = 90° (where the sin term integrates to zero) gives Um = −mB cos θ = −m·B. U is minimum, −mB, at θ = 0, the most stable position; it is maximum, +mB, at θ = 180°, the most unstable position; and it is zero at θ = 90°. The work required to turn the magnet from the stable to the unstable position is 2mB.

Numericals from this section are the commonest in the chapter. Read the angle carefully: the angle given is between m and B; if the question says the axis is perpendicular to the field, sin θ = 1. And keep the sign of U: a negative answer is correct at the stable position.

formulas.expr: τ = m × B, τ = mB sin θ
where: torque (N m); maximum mB at θ = 90°
moment of inertia of the needle about the axis of rotation (kg m<sup>2</sup>)
potential energy, zero at θ = 90°, −mB at θ = 0, +mB at θ = 180°
work done by an external agent in rotating from θ<sub>1</sub> to θ<sub>2</sub>

sections.tip: If the period question changes B to 4B, T halves; if it doubles m, T becomes T/√2. Students often invert these. Write ω² = mB/I first and then reason.

sections.heading: 5.2.4 The electrostatic analog
sections.body:
Compare the results for the bar magnet with those for the electric dipole in Chapter 1 and you will see that every magnetic formula is obtained from the electric one by three replacements: E → B, p → m and 1/ε0 → μ0. NCERT summarises this in Table 5.1, and reproducing that table is a safe 3-mark answer.

  • Equatorial field of a short dipole at distance r: electric E = −p/(4πε0r3); magnetic BE = −(μ0/4π) · m/r3. The minus sign says the field on the equatorial line is antiparallel to the moment.
  • Axial field: electric E = 2p/(4πε0r3); magnetic BA = (μ0/4π) · 2m/r3, parallel to m.
  • Torque in an external field: p × E and m × B.
  • Potential energy: −p·E and −m·B.

Both fields fall as 1/r3, and at the same distance the axial field is twice the equatorial field. The exact expressions for a magnet of half-length l are BA = (μ0/4π) · 2mr/(r2 − l2)2 and BE = (μ0/4π) · m/(r2 + l2)3/2; for r ≫ l these reduce to the forms above.

NCERT works Example 5.4 with this: a bar magnet of length 5.0 cm and moment 0.40 A m2, at 50 cm from its mid-point. Since l = 2.5 cm ≪ 50 cm, BE = 10−7 × 0.40/(0.5)3 = 3.2 × 10−7 T and BA = 6.4 × 10−7 T. The analogy also tells you what is not the same: an electric dipole is made of two real charges that can be separated, while the magnetic dipole cannot be split into monopoles, and inside the magnet the field runs S to N, along m, whereas inside an electric dipole the field runs opposite to p.

formulas.expr: B<sub>A</sub> = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π) · 2m/r<sup>3</sup> (along m); B<sub>E</sub> = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π) · m/r<sup>3</sup> (opposite to m)
where: distance from the centre of a short magnet, r ≫ l

sections.tip: A favourite MCQ: the ratio of the axial to the equatorial field at the same distance from a short magnet is 2:1. If the distance doubles, each field falls to one-eighth.

sections.heading: 5.3 Magnetism and Gauss's Law
sections.body:
In electrostatics, Gauss's law says that the flux of E through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε0. The magnetic version is simpler: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. In symbols, ΦB = ∮ B·ΔS = 0, where the sum runs over all the area elements of the closed surface.

The reason is in the field-line picture. Because magnetic field lines are closed loops, every line that enters a closed surface must also leave it. The number of lines going in equals the number coming out, so the net flux is zero, whatever surface you draw and wherever you draw it. Try it on a bar magnet: a closed surface around only the north pole has lines leaving through the outer part and the same lines entering through the part that cuts the magnet. Compare an electric dipole: a surface enclosing only the positive charge has net outward flux q/ε0, because the lines start on that charge.

The physical content of the law is that isolated magnetic poles, magnetic monopoles, do not exist. The simplest source of a magnetic field is a dipole (a current loop), not a magnetic charge. This is why the law has a zero on the right-hand side and why there is no magnetic equivalent of a point charge.

Two things are asked in the exam. First, state the law and give its meaning in one line. Second, a figure-based question: given a set of field-line diagrams, say which cannot represent a magnetic field. Any diagram in which lines start or end at a point in empty space, or in which the net flux out of a closed region is not zero, cannot be a magnetic field; it could be an electrostatic field with charges at those points. Diagrams with intersecting lines cannot represent either field.

formulas.expr: Φ<sub>B</sub> = ∮ B·ΔS = 0 for any closed surface
where: area element of the closed surface, outward normal

sections.tip: Write the law with the phrase 'any closed surface' and the reason 'because magnetic monopoles do not exist'. Both are marking points. Do not say the flux is zero because B is zero.

sections.heading: 5.4 Magnetisation and Magnetic Intensity
sections.body:
Every electron in an atom has an orbital magnetic moment and a spin magnetic moment, so each atom may have a net moment. In most materials these atomic moments point in random directions and cancel; in some they add up to a bulk moment. The magnetisation M of a sample is its net magnetic moment per unit volume, M = mnet/V, a vector with SI unit A m−1.

Now put a material inside a long solenoid of n turns per metre carrying current I. The field produced by the current alone is B0 = μ0nI. The material becomes magnetised and adds its own field Bm = μ0M (for a long, uniformly magnetised sample), so the total field inside is B = B0 + Bm = μ0(nI + M). It is convenient to define the magnetic intensity H = B/μ0 − M. H depends only on the free current in the windings, H = nI for the solenoid, and it has the same unit as M, A m−1. The total field is then B = μ0(H + M): H is the external contribution and M is the material's own contribution. Note the pattern, sometimes written as B = μ0(H + M) with M itself depending on H.

For most materials M is proportional to H: M = χH, where χ is the magnetic susceptibility, a dimensionless number that measures how easily the material is magnetised. Then B = μ0(1 + χ)H = μ0μrH = μH, with μr = 1 + χ the relative permeability (dimensionless) and μ = μ0μr the permeability of the material (T m A−1). The three quantities χ, μr and μ are not independent; give any one and the other two follow.

NCERT's worked example (Example 5.9 in the older text) is the template for the 3-mark numerical. A solenoid has 1000 turns per metre, current 2 A, and a core of μr = 400. Then H = nI = 2000 A m−1; B = μrμ0H = 400 × 4π × 10−7 × 2000 ≈ 1.0 T; M = (μr − 1)H ≈ 8 × 105 A m−1. The magnetising current Im, the extra current in the windings that would produce the same B without the core, satisfies M = nIm, so Im = 7.98 × 105/1000 ≈ 798 A (about 800 A). That number is the whole point: the core does the work of hundreds of amperes.

where: magnetisation, net magnetic moment per unit volume (A m<sup>−1</sup>)

formulas.expr: H = B/μ<sub>0</sub> − M; for a solenoid H = nI
where: magnetic intensity (A m<sup>−1</sup>), set by the free current only

formulas.expr: M = χH; B = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ)H = μ<sub>0</sub>μ<sub>r</sub>H = μH; μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ
where: permeability of the medium, μ = μ<sub>0</sub>μ<sub>r</sub> (T m A<sup>−1</sup>)

sections.tip: H does not change when the core is inserted; B and M do. If a question asks how B changes when a core of χ is placed in a toroid, answer B = μ0(1 + χ)H, so it rises by the fraction χ for a paramagnet and falls by |χ| for a diamagnet.

sections.heading: 5.5 Magnetic Properties of Materials
sections.body:
Materials are classified by their susceptibility χ. NCERT gives the ranges in one line each, and the same line is what the examiner wants when a question gives a value of χ or μr and asks you to identify the material.

  • Diamagnetic: −1 ≤ χ < 0, so 0 ≤ μr < 1 and μ < μ0. Small negative susceptibility; feebly repelled by a magnet.
  • Paramagnetic: 0 < χ < ε, so 1 < μr < 1 + ε and μ > μ0, where ε is a small positive number. Small positive susceptibility; feebly attracted.
  • Ferromagnetic: χ ≫ 1, so μr ≫ 1 and μ ≫ μ0. Large positive susceptibility (hundreds to thousands); strongly attracted.

So a material with μr = 0.9983 (χ = −0.0017) is diamagnetic, one with χ = 1.9 × 10−5 is paramagnetic, and one with μr = 400 is ferromagnetic. The rule is mechanical: negative means dia, small positive means para, large positive means ferro.

Three more distinctions carry the 2- and 3-mark questions. Field lines: in a diamagnetic sample the lines are pushed out and become sparser inside (the field inside is reduced); in a paramagnetic sample they are drawn in slightly and become denser inside; in a ferromagnetic sample they are pulled in strongly and crowd inside. Non-uniform field: a diamagnetic sample moves from the stronger to the weaker part of the field, while para- and ferromagnetic samples move from the weaker to the stronger part. A diamagnetic rod suspended freely sets itself perpendicular to the field; a paramagnetic rod sets itself along the field. Temperature: diamagnetism is almost independent of temperature; paramagnetic susceptibility falls as 1/T (Curie's law); a ferromagnet loses its ferromagnetism above the Curie temperature and becomes paramagnetic.

Learn a few examples from each class with their signs: Bi, Cu, Pb, Si, water, nitrogen (at STP), NaCl and diamond are diamagnetic; Al, Na, Ca, O2 (at STP), CuCl2, Pt and Cr are paramagnetic; Fe, Co, Ni, Gd and alloys such as Alnico are ferromagnetic. The order of magnitude of χ for dia- and paramagnets in NCERT's table is 10−5; a question that gives χ = −2.6 × 10−5 wants the word diamagnetic and two properties, and a question that gives χ = 2.6 × 10−5 wants paramagnetic.

formulas.expr: Diamagnetic: −1 ≤ χ < 0, 0 ≤ μ<sub>r</sub> < 1; Paramagnetic: 0 < χ < ε, 1 < μ<sub>r</sub> < 1 + ε; Ferromagnetic: χ ≫ 1, μ<sub>r</sub> ≫ 1
where: the link used to convert between the two

sections.tip: Always answer a classification question with the sign and size of χ, the value of μr, and one behaviour (repelled, feebly attracted, strongly attracted). Three columns, three rows, is the safest 3-mark answer in the chapter.

sections.heading: 5.5.1 Diamagnetism
sections.body:
Diamagnetic substances are those which tend to move from a stronger to a weaker part of an external magnetic field. In other words, they are feebly repelled by a magnet, the opposite of what iron does. When a diamagnetic rod is placed in a field, the field lines are expelled from it and the field inside is slightly reduced; a freely suspended diamagnetic rod sets itself perpendicular to the field. Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, nitrogen at STP, water and sodium chloride.

Mechanism. Electrons in an atom orbit the nucleus and each orbit is a tiny current loop with a magnetic moment. In a diamagnetic atom the moments of the electrons cancel, so the atom has no net moment. When an external field is applied, the electrons whose orbital moment is along the field slow down and those whose moment is opposite to the field speed up (this is Lenz's law at the atomic level, the same physics as electromagnetic induction). The result is a small net induced moment opposite to the applied field, and the material is repelled. Because the effect is induced and does not depend on any pre-existing atomic moment, it is present in every material, but it is masked when the atoms have permanent moments, as in para- and ferromagnets.

Since thermal motion does not affect an induced moment, diamagnetism is nearly independent of temperature. That one line answers the frequent 1-mark question.

Superconductors. Some metals cooled to very low temperatures show perfect conductivity and perfect diamagnetism: the field lines are completely expelled, χ = −1 and μr = 0. This is the Meissner effect, and it is why a magnet can be levitated above a superconductor. NCERT mentions that superconducting magnets are used in the fastest trains. The value χ = −1 is the lower limit of the diamagnetic range, which is why the range is written −1 ≤ χ < 0.

where: complete expulsion of the field from a superconductor; a perfect diamagnet

sections.tip: When you explain diamagnetism, say the induced moment is opposite to the field and cite Lenz's law. An answer that only says 'no net atomic moment' gets partial credit.

sections.heading: 5.5.2 Paramagnetism
sections.body:
Paramagnetic substances are those which get weakly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field, in the same direction as the field. They tend to move from a weaker to a stronger part of the field, so they are feebly attracted by a magnet. The field lines are drawn slightly into a paramagnetic sample and the field inside is slightly larger than outside. Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen at STP and copper chloride.

Mechanism. Each atom (or ion or molecule) of a paramagnetic material has a permanent magnetic dipole moment of its own, because the electron moments do not cancel. Without a field, thermal agitation keeps these moments randomly oriented and the net magnetisation is zero. An applied field B0 exerts a torque on each moment and tends to align it along the field; thermal motion fights this alignment. The balance gives a small net magnetisation along B0. A stronger field or a lower temperature improves the alignment, so the magnetisation grows with B0/T.

Curie's law. Experimentally, for not too strong fields and not too low temperatures, M = C B0/T, equivalently χ = C μ0/T, where C is the Curie constant of the material and T is the absolute temperature. The susceptibility of a paramagnet is therefore inversely proportional to temperature: cool the sample to half the absolute temperature and χ doubles. This is why a paramagnetic sample shows more magnetisation for the same field when cooled, a question asked directly in the exam.

Saturation. Curie's law cannot hold at very high fields or very low temperatures, because once every atomic dipole is aligned the magnetisation cannot grow any further. The magnetisation then saturates at Ms, the value when all moments point along the field. Note also the contrast with diamagnetism: diamagnetism comes from induced moments and ignores temperature; paramagnetism comes from permanent moments and is controlled by temperature.

formulas.expr: M = C B<sub>0</sub>/T, χ = C μ<sub>0</sub>/T (Curie's law)
where: applied field; valid for weak fields and high temperatures, before saturation

sections.tip: A quick numerical: if χ of a paramagnet is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ at 300 K, at 200 K it is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 300/200 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵. Use ratios; never plug in Celsius temperatures.

sections.heading: 5.5.3 Ferromagnetism
sections.body:
Ferromagnetic substances get strongly magnetised when placed in an external field, in the direction of the field. They move from the weaker to the stronger region and are strongly attracted by a magnet; the field lines crowd inside the sample and the field inside can be hundreds or thousands of times the applied field. Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and alloys like Alnico.

Mechanism: domains. As in a paramagnet, each atom has a permanent moment. In a ferromagnet, however, neighbouring atoms interact so strongly (the quantum-mechanical exchange interaction, which NCERT names but does not explain) that the moments of a large group of atoms align spontaneously. Such a region of uniform magnetisation is called a domain. A domain is about 1 mm across and contains about 1011 atoms, so each domain has a large moment. In an unmagnetised sample the domains are oriented randomly and their moments cancel. When a field is applied, the domains aligned with the field grow at the expense of the others, and the domains also rotate towards the field. The whole sample then acts as a giant magnet, which is why χ is so large.

Hard and soft. In some ferromagnets the magnetisation persists after the field is removed; these are hard ferromagnets (Alnico, used for permanent magnets). In others the magnetisation disappears once the field is removed; these are soft ferromagnets (soft iron, used for electromagnets and transformer cores). The hysteresis (B-H) loop that quantifies retentivity and coercivity has been removed from the rationalised syllabus, but you should still know the two words hard and soft.

Curie temperature. Heating a ferromagnet increases thermal agitation and disrupts the domain ordering. Above a characteristic temperature Tc, the Curie temperature, the domain structure disintegrates and the material becomes paramagnetic. In the paramagnetic phase above Tc, the susceptibility follows χ = C/(T − Tc), which is Curie's law with the temperature measured from Tc. NCERT tabulates: cobalt 1394 K, iron 1043 K, Fe2O3 893 K, nickel 631 K, gadolinium 317 K. An iron nail heated red hot is not attracted by a magnet, which is the everyday evidence.

NCERT's domain example (Example 5.10 in the older text) is worth reproducing: a cubic domain of iron of side 1 μm has volume 10−18 m3 = 10−12 cm3, mass 7.9 × 10−12 g (density 7.9 g cm−3), hence 7.9 × 10−12 × 6.023 × 1023/55 ≈ 8.65 × 1010 atoms. With 9.27 × 10−24 A m2 per atom, the maximum moment is 8.0 × 10−13 A m2 and the maximum magnetisation is 8.0 × 105 A m−1, the same order as the M found in the solenoid example.

formulas.expr: χ = C/(T − T<sub>c</sub>) for T > T<sub>c</sub>
where: Curie temperature; above it a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic

sections.tip: If asked why a ferromagnet has a much larger susceptibility than a paramagnet, the answer is domains: a large group of atomic moments is already aligned inside each domain, so the field has to align domains rather than individual atoms.

key_terms.definition: For a bar magnet, m = q<sub>m</sub> × 2l, directed from the south pole to the north pole inside the magnet; for a current loop, m = NIA along the normal by the right-hand rule. SI unit A m<sup>2</sup> or J T<sup>−1</sup>.

The quantity q<sub>m</sub> that characterises the strength of a magnetic pole; the force on a pole in a field is q<sub>m</sub>B. SI unit A m. Unchanged when a magnet is cut across its length, halved when cut along its length.
Continuous closed loops whose tangent gives the direction of B and whose density gives its magnitude; they run N to S outside a magnet and S to N inside, and never intersect.

key_terms.term: Axial and equatorial field of a short magnet
key_terms.definition: B<sub>A</sub> = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·2m/r<sup>3</sup> along m on the axis; B<sub>E</sub> = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·m/r<sup>3</sup> opposite to m on the perpendicular bisector; both for r ≫ l.
τ = m × B, magnitude mB sin θ, tending to align m with B; zero at θ = 0 and 180°, maximum mB at 90°.
U = −m·B = −mB cos θ, with zero at θ = 90°; minimum −mB at stable equilibrium (θ = 0) and maximum +mB at unstable equilibrium (θ = 180°).
The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, ∮B·ΔS = 0, because magnetic monopoles do not exist and field lines form closed loops.
The net magnetic moment per unit volume of a material, M = m<sub>net</sub>/V; a vector with SI unit A m<sup>−1</sup>.
H = B/μ<sub>0</sub> − M; the part of the field set by free currents alone, H = nI inside a solenoid, independent of the core material. SI unit A m<sup>−1</sup>.
The dimensionless ratio M = χH; negative and small for diamagnets, positive and small for paramagnets, large and positive for ferromagnets.
μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ = μ/μ<sub>0</sub>, dimensionless; less than 1 for diamagnets, slightly more than 1 for paramagnets, much more than 1 for ferromagnets.

Weak magnetisation opposite to the applied field, caused by moments induced in atoms with no net moment (Lenz's law); the sample is feebly repelled and moves to the weaker field; nearly independent of temperature.
Weak magnetisation along the applied field in materials whose atoms have permanent moments, partially aligned against thermal agitation; feebly attracted; χ ∝ 1/T (Curie's law).
Strong magnetisation along the field in materials such as Fe, Co, Ni, arising from domains in which atomic moments are already aligned; χ ≫ 1; lost above the Curie temperature.
A region of a ferromagnet, about 1 mm in size and containing about 10<sup>11</sup> atoms, in which all atomic moments are aligned; in an unmagnetised sample the domains point in random directions.
The temperature T<sub>c</sub> above which the domain structure of a ferromagnet breaks down and it behaves as a paramagnet with χ = C/(T − T<sub>c</sub>); 1043 K for iron, 631 K for nickel.
The complete expulsion of magnetic field lines from a superconductor, which therefore behaves as a perfect diamagnet with χ = −1 and μ<sub>r</sub> = 0.

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic moment of a bar magnet
formula_sheet.note: Directed S to N inside the magnet; unit A m<sup>2</sup> = J T<sup>−1</sup>. Cutting a magnet in any way halves m per piece; bending into a semicircle gives 2m/π.

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic moment of a solenoid or coil
formula_sheet.note: Along the axis by the right-hand rule; a solenoid of n turns per metre and length 2l has m = n(2l)I(πa<sup>2</sup>).

formula_sheet.name: Axial field of a short magnet
formula_sheet.note: r ≫ l; parallel to m. Exact: (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·2mr/(r<sup>2</sup> − l<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>.

formula_sheet.name: Equatorial field of a short magnet
formula_sheet.note: r ≫ l; antiparallel to m. Exact: (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·m/(r<sup>2</sup> + l<sup>2</sup>)<sup>3/2</sup>. B<sub>A</sub> = 2B<sub>E</sub> at the same r.

formula_sheet.name: Torque on a magnetic dipole
formula_sheet.expr: τ = m × B, τ = mB sin θ
formula_sheet.note: Uniform field: net force zero, torque aligns m with B; maximum mB at θ = 90°.

formula_sheet.name: Potential energy of a dipole
formula_sheet.note: Zero at 90°; −mB at stable, +mB at unstable equilibrium. Work from θ<sub>1</sub> to θ<sub>2</sub>: W = mB(cos θ<sub>1</sub> − cos θ<sub>2</sub>); stable to unstable: 2mB.

formula_sheet.name: Period of a compass needle
formula_sheet.note: Small oscillations in a uniform field; I is the moment of inertia about the pivot.

formula_sheet.name: Gauss's law for magnetism
formula_sheet.note: Any closed surface; expresses the non-existence of monopoles.

formula_sheet.name: Magnetisation and intensity
formula_sheet.expr: M = m<sub>net</sub>/V; H = B/μ<sub>0</sub> − M; B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M)
formula_sheet.note: Both M and H in A m<sup>−1</sup>. In a solenoid H = nI regardless of the core.

formula_sheet.name: Susceptibility and permeability
formula_sheet.expr: M = χH; B = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ)H = μ<sub>0</sub>μ<sub>r</sub>H = μH; μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ
formula_sheet.note: χ, μ<sub>r</sub> dimensionless; μ in T m A<sup>−1</sup>; μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup> T m A<sup>−1</sup>.

formula_sheet.name: Curie's law
formula_sheet.expr: M = C B<sub>0</sub>/T, χ = C μ<sub>0</sub>/T
formula_sheet.note: Paramagnets, weak fields and high T; above T<sub>c</sub> a ferromagnet obeys χ = C/(T − T<sub>c</sub>).

formula_sheet.name: Magnetising current
formula_sheet.note: The extra winding current that would give the same B as the core; in NCERT's example (μ<sub>r</sub> = 400, n = 1000 m<sup>−1</sup>, I = 2 A) I<sub>m</sub> ≈ 800 A.

diagrams.title: Field lines of a bar magnet and of a solenoid
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the bar magnet horizontally with N on the right and S on the left. Draw five or six closed loops that pass through the magnet: outside, arrows go from N round to S; inside the magnet, arrows go from S to N along the axis. Crowd the lines near the poles. Next to it draw a solenoid of the same length with current arrows on the turns, and the identical set of loops with the north face fixed by the right-hand rule. Caption both as dipole fields and note that the loops are continuous.

diagrams.title: Torque on a bar magnet in a uniform field
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw uniform parallel field lines B horizontally. Draw a magnet of length 2l at angle θ to B with m from S to N. At the N pole draw a force q<sub>m</sub>B along B; at the S pole a force q<sub>m</sub>B opposite to B. Mark the perpendicular distance between the two forces as 2l sin θ and write τ = q<sub>m</sub>B · 2l sin θ = mB sin θ. Show the sense of rotation towards B and state that the net force is zero.

diagrams.title: Field lines in dia-, para- and ferromagnetic samples
diagrams.how_to_draw: Three panels, each with a rectangular sample in a uniform field drawn as horizontal lines. Diamagnetic: lines bend around the sample and are fewer inside it. Paramagnetic: lines bend slightly into the sample and are a little denser inside. Ferromagnetic: lines are strongly pulled in and packed densely inside. Label each panel with the sign of χ and the range of μ<sub>r</sub>.

diagrams.title: Solenoid element for the equivalent-solenoid derivation
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a solenoid of length 2l and radius a with its centre at the origin and axis along x. Shade a thin slice of thickness dx at distance x from the centre and mark a point P on the axis at distance r from the centre, so that its distance from the slice is r − x. Write dB for the slice, then note r ≫ a and r ≫ l before integrating from −l to +l to get B = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·2m/r<sup>3</sup>.

diagrams.title: Magnetisation versus temperature for a paramagnet and a ferromagnet
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two small graphs. Left: χ against T for a paramagnet, a falling 1/T curve, labelled Curie's law. Right: M against T for a ferromagnet, roughly flat then dropping to zero at T<sub>c</sub>, labelled Curie temperature; beyond T<sub>c</sub> mark the material as paramagnetic. Axes labelled with units (T in kelvin).

ncert_questions.q: A short bar magnet placed with its axis at 30° with a uniform external magnetic field of 0.25 T experiences a torque of magnitude 4.5 × 10<sup>−2</sup> J. What is the magnitude of the magnetic moment of the magnet?

A short bar magnet of magnetic moment m = 0.32 J T<sup>−1</sup> is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.15 T. If the bar is free to rotate in the plane of the field, which orientation would correspond to its (a) stable, and (b) unstable equilibrium? What is the potential energy of the magnet in each case?
ncert_questions.a: U = −mB cos θ. (a) Stable equilibrium: m parallel to B, θ = 0. U = −mB = −0.32 × 0.15 = −4.8 × 10−2 J. (b) Unstable equilibrium: m antiparallel to B, θ = 180°. U = +mB = +4.8 × 10−2 J. In both positions the torque is zero, but a small displacement from (a) brings the magnet back while from (b) it moves further away.

ncert_questions.q: A closely wound solenoid of 800 turns and area of cross section 2.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> carries a current of 3.0 A. Explain the sense in which the solenoid acts like a bar magnet. What is its associated magnetic moment?
ncert_questions.a: The field of a current-carrying solenoid outside it is the same as that of a bar magnet: one face acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole, the field lines form closed loops, and the solenoid experiences a torque in an external field and aligns along it. Its magnetic moment is along the axis, in the sense given by the right-hand rule (fingers along the current, thumb towards the north face). Magnitude: m = NIA = 800 × 3.0 × 2.5 × 10−4 = 0.60 J T−1.

ncert_questions.q: If the solenoid in Exercise 5.3 is free to turn about the vertical direction and a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.25 T is applied, what is the magnitude of torque on the solenoid when its axis makes an angle of 30° with the direction of the applied field?

A bar magnet of magnetic moment 1.5 J T<sup>−1</sup> lies aligned with the direction of a uniform magnetic field of 0.22 T. (a) What is the amount of work required by an external torque to turn the magnet so as to align its magnetic moment (i) normal to the field direction, (ii) opposite to the field direction? (b) What is the torque on the magnet in cases (i) and (ii)?

A closely wound solenoid of 2000 turns and area of cross-section 1.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, carrying a current of 4.0 A, is suspended through its centre allowing it to turn in a horizontal plane. (a) What is the magnetic moment associated with the solenoid? (b) What is the force and torque on the solenoid if a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 7.5 × 10<sup>−2</sup> T is set up at an angle of 30° with the axis of the solenoid?
ncert_questions.a: (a) m = NIA = 2000 × 4.0 × 1.6 × 10−4 = 1.28 J T−1, along the axis of the solenoid. (b) In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero. Torque τ = mB sin θ = 1.28 × 7.5 × 10−2 × sin 30° = 1.28 × 0.075 × 0.5 = 4.8 × 10−2 N m, tending to align the axis with the field.

ncert_questions.q: A short bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 0.48 J T<sup>−1</sup>. Give the direction and magnitude of the magnetic field produced by the magnet at a distance of 10 cm from the centre of the magnet on (a) the axis, (b) the equatorial lines (normal bisector) of the magnet.
ncert_questions.a: r = 0.10 m, μ0/4π = 10−7 T m A−1. (a) Axial: BA = (μ0/4π) · 2m/r3 = 10−7 × 2 × 0.48/(0.10)3 = 10−7 × 0.96/10−3 = 0.96 × 10−4 T = 0.96 G, directed along the axis from the S pole to the N pole (along m). (b) Equatorial: BE = (μ0/4π) · m/r3 = 10−7 × 0.48/10−3 = 0.48 × 10−4 T = 0.48 G, directed opposite to m (from N to S, parallel to the axis).

ncert_questions.q: A magnetic needle has magnetic moment 6.7 × 10<sup>−2</sup> A m<sup>2</sup> and moment of inertia 7.5 × 10<sup>−6</sup> kg m<sup>2</sup>. It performs 10 complete oscillations in 6.70 s. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field?

A short bar magnet placed with its axis at 30° with an external field of 800 G experiences a torque of 0.016 N m. (a) What is the magnetic moment of the magnet? (b) What is the work done in moving it from its most stable to most unstable position? (c) The bar magnet is replaced by a solenoid of cross-sectional area 2 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> and 1000 turns, but of the same magnetic moment. Determine the current flowing through the solenoid.

(a) What happens if a bar magnet is cut into two pieces (i) transverse to its length, (ii) along its length? (b) A magnetised needle in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque but no net force. An iron nail near a bar magnet, however, experiences a force of attraction in addition to a torque. Why? (c) Must every magnetic configuration have a north pole and a south pole? What about the field due to a toroid? (d) Two identical looking iron bars A and B are given, one of which is definitely known to be magnetised. How would one ascertain whether or not both are magnetised? If only one is magnetised, how does one ascertain which one?
ncert_questions.a: (a) In either case you get two magnets, each with a north and a south pole. Cut transversely, each piece has the same pole strength and half the length, so half the moment; cut along the length, each has half the pole strength and the same length, again half the moment (a sharp transverse cut also leaves the pole strength slightly less than before, in practice). (b) The field of a bar magnet is non-uniform; the nail becomes magnetised with the induced pole nearer the magnet being the unlike pole, and in a non-uniform field the two poles of the nail feel unequal forces, so there is a net force of attraction along with a torque. (c) No. Poles exist only for a configuration whose external field resembles a dipole. A toroid has no poles at all; its field is confined within it, and the field of a straight infinite solenoid also has no poles. (d) Bring one end of A near an end of B and note the force, then bring the same end of A near the other end of B. If the force changes from attraction to repulsion, both bars are magnetised. If only one is magnetised, place the end of A against the middle of B; if there is attraction, A is the magnet (a magnet's end attracts the middle of an unmagnetised bar, but an unmagnetised bar's end feels no force at the neutral middle of a magnet).

ncert_questions.q: What is the magnitude of the equatorial and axial fields due to a bar magnet of length 5.0 cm at a distance of 50 cm from its mid-point? The magnetic moment of the bar magnet is 0.40 A m<sup>2</sup>.
ncert_questions.a: l = 2.5 cm ≪ r = 50 cm, so use the short-magnet formulas. BE = (μ0/4π)·m/r3 = 10−7 × 0.40/(0.5)3 = 10−7 × 0.40/0.125 = 3.2 × 10−7 T. BA = (μ0/4π)·2m/r3 = 2 × 3.2 × 10−7 = 6.4 × 10−7 T.

ncert_questions.q: A solenoid has a core of a material with relative permeability 400. The windings of the solenoid are insulated from the core and carry a current of 2 A. If the number of turns is 1000 per metre, calculate (a) H, (b) M, (c) B and (d) the magnetising current I<sub>m</sub>.
ncert_questions.a: (a) H = nI = 1000 × 2 = 2 × 103 A m−1. (b) M = χH = (μr − 1)H = 399 × 2000 ≈ 8 × 105 A m−1. (c) B = μrμ0H = 400 × 4π × 10−7 × 2000 = 1.0 T (1.005 T). (d) The magnetising current is the additional winding current that would produce the same B in the absence of the core: B = μ0n(I + Im), so M = nIm and Im = M/n = 7.98 × 105/1000 ≈ 798 A (about 800 A). The core is doing the work of hundreds of amperes.

ncert_questions.q: A domain in ferromagnetic iron is in the form of a cube of side length 1 μm. Estimate the number of iron atoms in the domain and the maximum possible dipole moment and magnetisation of the domain. The molecular mass of iron is 55 g mol<sup>−1</sup> and its density is 7.9 g cm<sup>−3</sup>. Assume that each iron atom has a dipole moment of 9.27 × 10<sup>−24</sup> A m<sup>2</sup>.
ncert_questions.a: Volume V = (10−6)3 = 10−18 m3 = 10−12 cm3. Mass = 7.9 × 10−12 g. Number of atoms N = (7.9 × 10−12/55) × 6.023 × 1023 ≈ 8.65 × 1010. Maximum moment (all atoms aligned) mmax = 8.65 × 1010 × 9.27 × 10−24 ≈ 8.0 × 10−13 A m2. Maximum magnetisation Mmax = mmax/V = 8.0 × 10−13/10−18 = 8.0 × 105 A m−1.

pyq.q: The relative permeability of a material is 0.9983. The material is
pyq.solution: μ<sub>r</sub> < 1 means χ = μ<sub>r</sub> − 1 = −0.0017 is negative and small, the signature of a diamagnetic material. (Asked as a 1-mark question in the 2011 Delhi paper.)

pyq.q: Out of the following, identify the pair of materials that are both diamagnetic: Bi, Al, Na, Cu, Ca, Ni.
pyq.solution: Bismuth and copper have negative susceptibility. Al, Na and Ca are paramagnetic; Ni is ferromagnetic.

pyq.q: At the same distance r from the centre of a short bar magnet, the ratio of the magnitude of the magnetic field on the axis to that on the equatorial line is
A bar magnet of magnetic moment m is cut into two equal halves along its length. The magnetic moment of each half is
pyq.solution: Cutting along the length halves the cross-section and hence the pole strength, while the length 2l is unchanged, so m' = (q<sub>m</sub>/2) × 2l = m/2.

pyq.q: The magnetic susceptibility of a superconductor is
pyq.solution: A superconductor expels the field completely (Meissner effect), so B = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ)H = 0 requires χ = −1; it is a perfect diamagnet with μ<sub>r</sub> = 0.

pyq.q: A magnetic dipole is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The potential energy of the dipole is minimum when the angle between the dipole moment and the field is
pyq.solution: U = −mB cos θ is least, equal to −mB, at θ = 0, the position of stable equilibrium.

pyq.q: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is
options: proportional to the pole strength enclosed
equal to the flux through its largest face
pyq.solution: Gauss's law for magnetism: field lines are closed loops and monopoles do not exist, so as many lines leave a closed surface as enter it.

pyq.q: A compass needle oscillates with period T in a uniform magnetic field B. If the field is increased to 4B, the period becomes
pyq.solution: T = 2π√(I/mB) ∝ 1/√B, so quadrupling B halves the period.

pyq.q: The magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material at 300 K is 2.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Its value at 150 K is approximately
pyq.solution: Curie's law: χ ∝ 1/T. Halving the absolute temperature doubles χ, giving 4.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Magnetic field lines always form closed loops. Reason (R): Magnetic monopoles do not exist.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.solution: Because there are no isolated poles for lines to begin or end on, every field line closes on itself; R is exactly the reason for A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The susceptibility of a diamagnetic material is almost independent of temperature. Reason (R): Diamagnetism arises from magnetic moments induced in the atoms by the applied field, not from permanent atomic moments.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.solution: Thermal agitation randomises permanent moments, which is why paramagnetism depends on T; an induced moment has no orientation to randomise, so diamagnetism does not.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The net magnetic flux through a closed surface enclosing the north pole of a bar magnet is zero. Reason (R): The magnetic field of a bar magnet is uniform.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.solution: The flux is zero by Gauss's law for magnetism (closed field lines), so A is true. The field of a bar magnet is not uniform; it falls as 1/r<sup>3</sup> far away, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A ferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic when heated above its Curie temperature. Reason (R): Above the Curie temperature, thermal agitation destroys the domain structure.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.solution: Ferromagnetism depends on ordered domains; once thermal energy breaks them up, the atomic moments behave independently and the material follows χ = C/(T − T<sub>c</sub>).

pyq.q: Define magnetic susceptibility of a material. Name two elements, one having positive susceptibility and the other having negative susceptibility. What does negative susceptibility signify?
pyq.answer: Magnetic susceptibility χ is the ratio of the magnetisation M produced in a material to the magnetic intensity H that produces it: χ = M/H. It is dimensionless. Positive susceptibility: aluminium (or calcium, sodium). Negative susceptibility: bismuth (or copper). A negative susceptibility means the magnetisation is opposite to the applied field, i.e. the material is diamagnetic: it is feebly repelled by a magnet and moves from the stronger to the weaker part of a field.

pyq.q: How does a diamagnetic material behave when it is cooled to very low temperatures? Mention how a diamagnetic sample and a paramagnetic sample behave when placed in a non-uniform magnetic field.
pyq.answer: Cooling has almost no effect on an ordinary diamagnet, because its induced moment does not depend on thermal motion; certain metals, however, become superconductors at very low temperature and then behave as perfect diamagnets (χ = −1), expelling the field completely. In a non-uniform field a diamagnetic sample moves from the stronger to the weaker region (it is repelled), while a paramagnetic sample moves from the weaker to the stronger region (it is attracted).

pyq.q: A circular coil of N turns and radius R carries a current I. It is unwound and rewound to make another coil of radius R/2, the current I remaining the same. Calculate the ratio of the magnetic moments of the new coil and the original coil.
pyq.answer: Length of wire is fixed: N × 2πR = N' × 2π(R/2), so N' = 2N. Original moment m1 = NIπR2. New moment m2 = N'Iπ(R/2)2 = 2N × I × πR2/4 = NIπR2/2. Ratio m2 : m1 = 1 : 2.

pyq.q: Draw the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet and state any two properties of these lines.
pyq.answer: Sketch: closed loops passing through the magnet, N to S outside and S to N inside, crowded at the poles. Properties (any two): (i) they form continuous closed loops, unlike electrostatic field lines; (ii) the tangent at a point gives the direction of B there; (iii) the number of lines per unit area is proportional to the magnitude of B; (iv) two field lines never intersect, since the field cannot have two directions at one point.

pyq.q: A bar magnet of length L and magnetic moment m is bent into a semicircle. What is its new magnetic moment?
pyq.answer: Bending does not change the pole strength qm = m/L. The arc length L = πR gives radius R = L/π, and the poles are now at the ends of the diameter, 2R = 2L/π apart. New moment m' = qm × 2R = (m/L)(2L/π) = 2m/π, about 0.64 m.

pyq.q: Why does a paramagnetic sample display greater magnetisation, for the same magnetising field, when cooled? Why is diamagnetism, in contrast, almost independent of temperature?
pyq.answer: Paramagnetic atoms have permanent moments that thermal agitation keeps disordered; cooling reduces the agitation, so the field aligns a larger fraction of the moments and M rises (Curie's law, M ∝ B0/T). In a diamagnet the atoms have no permanent moment; the moment is induced by the field itself and is the same in every atom whatever its thermal motion, so the effect does not change with temperature.

pyq.q: Derive an expression for the torque acting on a magnetic dipole placed in a uniform magnetic field. Hence obtain the expression for its potential energy and state the orientations of stable and unstable equilibrium.
pyq.answer: Consider a magnet of pole strength qm and length 2l, moment m = qm·2l, with m at angle θ to a uniform field B. The N pole feels a force qmB along B and the S pole an equal force opposite to B: net force zero, but the pair forms a couple with arm 2l sin θ. Torque τ = qmB × 2l sin θ = mB sin θ; in vector form τ = m × B, directed so as to align m with B. Work done by an external agent in rotating the dipole from θ1 to θ2: W = ∫mB sin θ dθ = mB(cos θ1 − cos θ2). Taking U = 0 at θ = 90°, U = −mB cos θ = −m·B. Stable equilibrium at θ = 0 (U = −mB, τ = 0, restoring torque on displacement); unstable equilibrium at θ = 180° (U = +mB, τ = 0, but a displacement grows).

pyq.q: A solenoid of 500 turns per metre carrying a current of 1.5 A has a core of relative permeability 600. Calculate (a) the magnetic intensity H, (b) the magnetisation M, and (c) the magnetic field B inside the core.

Distinguish between diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances on the basis of (i) magnetic susceptibility, (ii) relative permeability, and (iii) behaviour of magnetic field lines when a sample is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Give one example of each.
pyq.answer: Diamagnetic: (i) χ small and negative, −1 ≤ χ < 0; (ii) 0 ≤ μr < 1; (iii) field lines are expelled and become sparser inside the sample; example Bi, Cu. Paramagnetic: (i) χ small and positive, 0 < χ < ε; (ii) 1 < μr < 1 + ε; (iii) field lines are drawn slightly in and become a little denser inside; example Al, Ca. Ferromagnetic: (i) χ large and positive, χ ≫ 1; (ii) μr ≫ 1, of order 103 to 105; (iii) field lines are strongly concentrated inside the sample; example Fe, Ni, Co. Add the sketches of the three samples in a field for full marks.

pyq.q: State Gauss's law for magnetism. How is it different from Gauss's law in electrostatics? What physical fact does the difference express?
pyq.answer: Gauss's law for magnetism: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, ∮B·ΔS = 0. In electrostatics the flux of E through a closed surface equals qenclosed/ε0, which can be non-zero because electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges and an isolated charge can be enclosed. Magnetic field lines are closed loops, so every line entering a closed surface also leaves it and the net flux is always zero. The difference expresses the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist: the simplest magnetic source is a dipole, and cutting a magnet only produces smaller dipoles.

pyq.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 2.0 A m<sup>2</sup> is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T with its moment along the field. Find (a) the work done in rotating it through 60°, (b) the torque on it in the new position, and (c) the additional work needed to bring it to the position of unstable equilibrium.

Show that a compass needle free to rotate in a horizontal plane, placed in a uniform magnetic field, executes simple harmonic motion for small angular displacements. Derive the expression for its time period and hence for the magnetic field.
pyq.answer: Let the needle have moment m and moment of inertia I about the pivot, and let it be displaced by a small angle θ from the field B. The torque on it is τ = −mB sin θ, the negative sign showing that it is restoring. By the rotational equation of motion, I d2θ/dt2 = −mB sin θ. For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, so d2θ/dt2 = −(mB/I)θ. The angular acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction, which is the defining condition for SHM, with ω2 = mB/I. Hence T = 2π/ω = 2π√(I/mB). Squaring, T2 = 4π2I/(mB), so B = 4π2I/(mT2). Measuring T with a needle of known m and I gives the field.

pyq.q: Derive an expression for the magnetic field on the axis of a current-carrying solenoid at a point far from it, and hence show that a solenoid is equivalent to a bar magnet. Write the electrostatic analog of the axial field expression.
pyq.answer: Consider a solenoid of radius a, length 2l, n turns per unit length and current I, centred at the origin with its axis along x. A slice of thickness dx at distance x from the centre has n dx turns and acts as a circular coil. Its field at a point P on the axis at distance r from the centre is dB = μ0(n dx)I a2/2[(r − x)2 + a2]3/2. For a distant point, r ≫ a and r ≫ l, so (r − x)2 + a2 ≈ r2 and dB ≈ μ0nIa2 dx/2r3. Integrating over x from −l to +l: B = μ0nIa2(2l)/2r3. Writing this as B = (μ0/4π)·2[n(2l)I(πa2)]/r3 = (μ0/4π)·2m/r3, with m = n(2l)Iπa2 = NIA. This is identical to the axial field of a bar magnet of moment m, so the solenoid is equivalent to a bar magnet with moment NIA along its axis, north face by the right-hand rule. The equivalence also shows in experiment: a suspended solenoid aligns N-S and attracts or repels a magnet. Electrostatic analog: the axial field of an electric dipole is E = 2p/(4πε0r3), obtained by p → m, 1/ε0 → μ0, E → B.

pyq.q: Define magnetisation, magnetic intensity, magnetic susceptibility and relative permeability of a material and obtain the relations among them. Using these, classify materials as diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic, and state how the susceptibility of each varies with temperature.
pyq.answer: Magnetisation M is the net magnetic moment per unit volume of a material, M = mnet/V (A m−1). Inside a solenoid of n turns per metre carrying I with a core, the field is B = B0 + Bm = μ0nI + μ0M. The magnetic intensity is defined as H = B/μ0 − M, so that H = nI depends only on the free current (A m−1) and B = μ0(H + M). For most materials M = χH, where the dimensionless χ is the magnetic susceptibility. Then B = μ0(1 + χ)H = μ0μrH = μH, where μr = 1 + χ is the relative permeability and μ = μ0μr the permeability. Classification: diamagnetic, −1 ≤ χ < 0, 0 ≤ μr < 1, feebly repelled (Bi, Cu); paramagnetic, 0 < χ < ε, 1 < μr < 1 + ε, feebly attracted (Al, Ca); ferromagnetic, χ ≫ 1, μr ≫ 1, strongly attracted (Fe, Ni, Co). Temperature: diamagnetic χ is nearly independent of T; paramagnetic χ = Cμ0/T (Curie's law) falls with T; ferromagnetic χ falls with T and above the Curie temperature Tc the material becomes paramagnetic with χ = C/(T − Tc).

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Materials respond to a magnetic field according to their susceptibility χ, defined by M = χH. Diamagnetic materials such as bismuth and copper have small negative χ; their atoms have no permanent moment, and the field induces a moment opposite to itself. Paramagnetic materials such as aluminium have small positive χ; their atoms have permanent moments that the field partly aligns against thermal agitation, and χ ∝ 1/T. Ferromagnetic materials such as iron have very large χ because their atomic moments are already aligned within domains; above the Curie temperature the domains break up. A superconductor expels the field completely and is a perfect diamagnet.
(i) Which of the three classes of material moves towards the weaker region of a non-uniform field?
(ii) What are the values of χ and μr for a superconductor?
(iii) The susceptibility of a paramagnetic salt is 3.0 × 10−4 at 300 K. What is it at 100 K?
(iv) Iron has a Curie temperature of 1043 K. Describe its magnetic behaviour at 1200 K.
pyq.answer: (i) Diamagnetic materials; they are repelled and move from the stronger to the weaker field. (ii) χ = −1 and μr = 1 + χ = 0. (iii) Curie's law χ ∝ 1/T: χ = 3.0 × 10−4 × 300/100 = 9.0 × 10−4. (iv) Above 1043 K the domain structure is destroyed, so at 1200 K iron is paramagnetic: weakly magnetised along the field, with a small positive χ that obeys χ = C/(T − Tc).

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field whose pattern outside is the same as that of a bar magnet. Far from the solenoid, the field on its axis is B = (μ0/4π)·2m/r3, where m = NIA is the magnetic moment (N turns, current I, area A). Placed in a uniform external field B, the solenoid experiences no net force but a torque τ = mB sin θ, and has potential energy U = −mB cos θ. A solenoid has 500 turns, cross-sectional area 4.0 × 10−4 m2 and carries 2.0 A.
(i) Calculate the magnetic moment of the solenoid.
(ii) Find the torque on it when its axis is perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.20 T.
(iii) What is its potential energy when its axis is along the field?
(iv) If the current is reversed, what happens to the poles of the solenoid and to its magnetic moment?
pyq.answer: (i) m = NIA = 500 × 2.0 × 4.0 × 10−4 = 0.40 A m2. (ii) θ = 90°: τ = mB = 0.40 × 0.20 = 0.080 N m. (iii) θ = 0: U = −mB = −0.080 J. (iv) The north and south faces interchange; the magnetic moment keeps the same magnitude 0.40 A m2 but reverses direction.

practice_mcq.q: The SI unit of magnetic dipole moment is
practice_mcq.explanation: m = NIA has unit A m<sup>2</sup>, equivalently J T<sup>−1</sup> from U = −mB.

practice_mcq.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment m is cut into two equal pieces transverse to its length. The pole strength of each piece is
practice_mcq.explanation: A transverse cut keeps the cross-section, so the pole strength is unchanged; it is the length, and so the moment, that halves.

practice_mcq.q: The magnetic field on the axis of a short bar magnet at a distance r from its centre is B. At a distance 2r on the axis the field is
practice_mcq.explanation: B<sub>A</sub> ∝ 1/r<sup>3</sup>, so doubling r divides the field by 8.

practice_mcq.q: The torque on a magnetic dipole in a uniform field is maximum when the angle between m and B is
practice_mcq.explanation: τ = mB sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, at 90°.

practice_mcq.q: The work done in turning a magnet of moment m from the position of stable equilibrium to that of unstable equilibrium in a field B is
The SI unit of magnetisation M and of magnetic intensity H is
practice_mcq.explanation: M is moment per unit volume, A m<sup>2</sup>/m<sup>3</sup> = A m<sup>−1</sup>; H = nI has the same unit.

practice_mcq.q: The relation between relative permeability and susceptibility is
practice_mcq.explanation: B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M) = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ)H = μ<sub>0</sub>μ<sub>r</sub>H gives μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ.

practice_mcq.q: A material has magnetic susceptibility 2.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. It is
practice_mcq.explanation: A small positive susceptibility is the signature of a paramagnet (this is the value NCERT lists for aluminium).

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a ferromagnetic material?
practice_mcq.explanation: Nickel, like iron and cobalt, has domains and a very large susceptibility; Bi and Cu are diamagnetic, Al is paramagnetic.

practice_mcq.q: When a diamagnetic rod is suspended freely in a uniform magnetic field, it comes to rest
practice_mcq.explanation: The induced moment is opposite to the field, so the rod is repelled and sets itself perpendicular to the field, unlike a paramagnetic rod which aligns along it.

practice_mcq.q: According to Curie's law, the susceptibility of a paramagnetic material varies with absolute temperature T as
practice_mcq.explanation: χ = Cμ<sub>0</sub>/T: thermal agitation opposes alignment, so a lower T gives a larger χ.

practice_mcq.q: A ferromagnetic material is heated above its Curie temperature. It becomes
practice_mcq.explanation: The domain structure disintegrates above T<sub>c</sub>, leaving independent atomic moments, i.e. a paramagnet with χ = C/(T − T<sub>c</sub>).

practice_mcq.q: A solenoid with an air core carries a steady current. A rod of relative permeability 400 is now inserted as the core. Which quantity is unchanged?
practice_mcq.explanation: H = nI is fixed by the winding current alone; B and M rise roughly 400-fold with the core.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following statements about magnetic field lines is false?
options: Their tangent gives the direction of B
They start on a north pole and end on a south pole
practice_mcq.explanation: Lines do not start or end anywhere; outside a magnet they run N to S but continue inside from S to N, forming closed loops.

practice_mcq.q: A magnetic needle of moment m and moment of inertia I oscillates with period T in a field B. Another needle of moment 2m and moment of inertia 2I in the same field oscillates with period
practice_mcq.explanation: T = 2π√(I/mB); doubling both I and m leaves I/m, and so T, unchanged.

practice_mcq.q: The magnetic field at a point on the equatorial line of a short magnet is directed
options: perpendicular to the axis, away from the magnet
perpendicular to the axis, towards the magnet
practice_mcq.explanation: B<sub>E</sub> = −(μ<sub>0</sub>/4π)·m/r<sup>3</sup>: the field on the perpendicular bisector is antiparallel to m, just as for the electric dipole.

practice_mcq.q: Approximately how many atoms does a single domain in a ferromagnet contain, according to NCERT?
practice_mcq.explanation: A domain is about 1 mm across and holds about 10<sup>11</sup> atoms, all with aligned moments.

common_mistakes: Drawing the field lines of a bar magnet only outside the magnet, as though they start at N and end at S. Magnetic lines are closed loops; the examiner looks for the S-to-N lines inside the magnet and deducts for their absence.
Using the geometric angle of the magnet with the vertical or with a wire instead of the angle between m and B in τ = mB sin θ. If the axis is perpendicular to the field, sin θ = 1, not 0.
Dropping the minus sign in U = −mB cos θ, or reporting the potential energy at stable equilibrium as +mB. The stable position has the lowest, negative, energy.
Mixing up the two cuts. Transverse cut: pole strength same, length halves. Lengthwise cut: pole strength halves, length same. Both give m/2, but the reasoning is what is marked in a 2-mark question.

Writing μ<sub>r</sub> = χ or μ = μ<sub>0</sub>χ. The correct links are μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ and μ = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ). A material with μ<sub>r</sub> = 0.9983 has χ = −0.0017 and is diamagnetic, not paramagnetic.
Classifying a material with a small negative susceptibility as non-magnetic. Every material responds to a field; small negative means diamagnetic.

Saying that diamagnetism increases on cooling in the way paramagnetism does. Diamagnetism is nearly temperature independent; only the special case of superconductivity appears at very low temperature.
Using Celsius temperatures in Curie's law ratios. χ ∝ 1/T needs kelvin: 27 °C is 300 K.
Forgetting that H does not change when a core is inserted into a solenoid. H = nI; it is B and M that change with the core.

strategy:
This chapter is small and the questions are predictable, so aim to lose nothing here. Start with the dipole physics of Section 5.2: learn the four properties of field lines, the two field formulas (axial twice the equatorial, both falling as 1/r3), and be able to derive τ = mB sin θ, U = −mB cos θ and T = 2π√(I/mB) on a blank page. Practise the NCERT exercises 5.1 to 5.7; they are the numericals the board recycles, and each takes under three minutes once the formulas are automatic.

Next, the materials part. Make a three-row table (dia, para, ferro) with columns for χ, μr, field-line behaviour, motion in a non-uniform field, temperature dependence, and two examples, and reproduce it from memory. Add the mechanism in one sentence for each: induced moment opposing the field (Lenz), permanent moments partly aligned against thermal agitation (Curie's law), and domains (Curie temperature). Know that a superconductor has χ = −1.

Then Section 5.4: write the chain M = χH, B = μ0(H + M) = μ0(1 + χ)H = μH, μr = 1 + χ, and work the solenoid-with-core example so that you can find H, M, B and Im quickly. Finally, be able to state Gauss's law for magnetism with its meaning in one line.

On the day: 1-mark questions from this chapter should take under a minute each; classification questions are worth answering in a table; for the 5-mark derivations, write the assumptions (small angle; r ≫ a and r ≫ l) explicitly. Skip the earth's magnetism and hysteresis material in old question banks; it is no longer in the syllabus.
